title: Count Non-Decreasing Subarrays After K Operations
statement:
`nums` is an integer array and `k` is a positive integer. Consider each contiguous, non-empty subarray of `nums` separately, always starting from the original values: an operation adds 1 to one element of that subarray, and at most `k` operations may be used on it.

Return how many subarrays can be made non-decreasing this way, meaning every element ends up at least as large as the one before it.
notes:
## Intuition

The cheapest fix raises each element to its running maximum (the largest value up to it), so a subarray costs the sum of running maximum minus value. Trying every subarray is O(n²).

The cost grows when the subarray gains an element on the right and shrinks when it loses its first one. So for each right end the working left ends form a range whose start never moves back: a sliding window. The hard part is the left end leaving, since it may have been the running maximum of a whole stretch.

## Approach

1. A monotonic stack finds `nextAtLeast[i]`, the first later index whose value is at least `nums[i]`, and `takeOver[p]`, the indices whose nearest strictly larger value on the left is `p`. These are the new running maxima once `p` is gone.
2. Move `right` across `nums`. The deque `maxQueue` (read from `head`) holds the window's maximum, so adding `nums[right]` costs `nums[maxQueue[head]] - nums[right]`.
3. While `cost > k`, drop `left`. Each `i` in `takeOver[left]` up to `right` becomes the running maximum of positions `i` to `min(nextAtLeast[i], right + 1) - 1`, saving `nums[left] - nums[i]` on each. Advance `left`, and `head` if it pointed there.
4. Every start from `left` to `right` works, so add `right - left + 1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [6,3,1,2,4,4]`, `k = 7`. Windows `[6]` and `[6,3]` cost 0 and 3, adding 1 and 2. Taking in the 1 raises the cost by 5 to 8, over 7, so 6 leaves: index 1 (value 3) takes over positions 1 and 2, saving `(6 - 3) · 2 = 6`. Window `[3,1]` costs 2 and adds 2. It then grows to `[3,1,2,4,4]`, whose cost stays at 3, adding 3, 4 and 5. The total is `1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 17`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index enters and leaves the stack and the deque once, and sits in at most one `takeOver` list.
- Space: O(n) for the lists, the stack and the deque.

## Pitfalls

- The cost is not the sum of drops between neighbours: `[3,1,2]` needs `2 + 1 = 3` operations, because 2 must also reach 3.
- When the first element leaves, every position it dominated gets cheaper, not just its own (which cost 0).
- Stop each stretch at the next value that is at least as large; stopping only at larger values counts equal values twice.
- The count can pass 2^31, so Java and C need 64-bit integers.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `nextAtLeast[i]` | first index after `i` with a value at least `nums[i]` (`n` if none) |
| `takeOver[p]` | indices whose nearest strictly larger value on the left is `p` |
| `stack` | indices still waiting for their `nextAtLeast` |
| `maxQueue`, `head` | window indices with decreasing values; `maxQueue[head]` is the maximum |
| `left`, `right` | the window's ends |
| `cost` | operations that make `nums[left..right]` non-decreasing |
| `count` | subarrays counted so far |

narration.3: By default no later value is at least nums[i], so its stretch runs to the end.
narration.4: takeOver[p] will list the indices that become running maxima once p leaves the window.
narration.6: Scan left to right, keeping a stack of indices whose values decrease.
narration.7: Each stacked value no larger than nums[i] has found its next value that is at least as big.
narration.8: Record i as that index's nextAtLeast and pop it.
narration.10: Whatever remains on top is the nearest strictly larger value left of i.
narration.11: So i takes over as the running maximum when that index leaves.
narration.21: Grow the window one element at a time to the right.
narration.22: Deque entries no larger than the new value can never be the maximum again...
narration.25: The new index joins the back of the deque.
narration.26: The new element must rise to the window's maximum, found at the deque's head.
narration.27: Too many operations: shrink the window from the left.
narration.28: Visit the indices that take over from the leaving element...
narration.29: ...but only those already inside the window.
narration.30: Positions from i up to its next at-least-as-large value now rise only to nums[i], saving nums[left] - nums[i] each.
narration.32: The old left end is gone.
narration.33: If the maximum was the old left end, the next deque entry becomes the maximum.
narration.35: Every start from left to right gives a subarray ending at right that can be fixed.
narration.37: Return the number of subarrays counted.
